hints: Look closely at the diagram. Can you spot the small glycerol backbone on the left and the three very long zig-zag tails on the right? Notice there is no free polar head left.
Think about what those long tails are made of, lots of C-C and C-H bonds, and what happens when many of those bonds are oxidised in respiration.
walkthrough:
**Read the diagram like a biologist**

Look left to right. On the left you have glycerol (CH2, CH, CH2) joined by three ester bonds (-O-C=O) to three fatty acids.

Those fatty acids are the long zig-zag hydrocarbon chains on the right. There is no hydrophilic phosphate head, so the whole molecule is non-polar and hydrophobic.

**Link structure to energy storage**

The key feature for function is those three long hydrocarbon tails. They contain a huge number of C-H bonds.

When oxidised in aerobic respiration, each C-H bond releases energy, so per gram a triglyceride releases about twice as much energy as carbohydrate.

**Check the location and role**

Because it is completely hydrophobic, triglycerides cluster together excluding water to form oil droplets in the cytoplasm of adipose and liver cells, not in membranes and not in lysosomes.

That points us clearly to D as the only statement that correctly links long hydrocarbon chains to high energy yield.

options.A: False. The glycerol is already ester-bonded to three fatty acids, so there is no free hydrophilic head to hydrogen bond with water. Oil droplets form because triglycerides are hydrophobic and exclude water.
options.B: False. Selective permeability of the cell surface membrane is due to the phospholipid bilayer, not triglycerides. Triglycerides are storage lipids and are not part of membranes.
options.C: False. Triglycerides do pack closely as energy reserves, but they are stored as oil droplets in the cytoplasm of adipose cells, not in lysosomes which contain hydrolytic enzymes.
options.D: Correct. The three long hydrocarbon fatty acid chains contain many C-H bonds which release a large amount of energy when oxidised, giving triglycerides a very high energy output per unit mass.
